summary: Defines CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures, a signature format that can stay valid for a long time, including evidence of validity even if a party later tries to deny it. It extends the Cryptographic Message Syntax. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A signature on paper can fade, but this kind keeps proof it was real for years. Nobody can later say it was not theirs.

questions: what is the difference between cades-t and cades-c
how do long term electronic signatures stay valid
subtitle: A signature format built on CMS that can still be proven valid years later, even if someone denies having signed.

tldr.problem: A digital signature depends on certificates, revocation data and algorithms that expire, get revoked or weaken over time, so a signature can become hard to trust or prove long after it was made.
tldr.mechanism: CAdES extends CMS signed data with extra signed and unsigned attributes. A basic signature can be built up with trusted time-stamps, references to or copies of certificates and revocation data, and finally archive time-stamps, forming a ladder of formats from CAdES-BES to CAdES-A.
tldr.outcome: The result is evidence usable in a later dispute. The RFC is Informational, a transposition of ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.7.4 that is technically equivalent to it, and it obsoletes RFC 3126.

today: RFC 5126 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 3126. No later RFC is listed as replacing or updating it, and the RFC says the technical contents are maintained by ETSI.

sections.title: Goal and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC covers electronic signatures for transactions where long-term validity matters, such as purchase requisitions, contracts and invoices. The aim is evidence of validity even if the signer or the verifying party later attempts to deny (repudiate) the signature. It applies between individuals, companies and governmental bodies, and is independent of the environment, for example smart cards or special signing programs.

The scope is signature formats only. Signature policies are defined elsewhere (RFC 3125 and an ETSI report). The formats build on CMS (RFC 3852), X.509, the PKIX certificate profile (RFC 3280) and the time-stamp protocol (RFC 3161), and are described in ASN.1. The name CAdES stands for CMS Advanced Electronic Signatures. Its sibling for XML is XAdES.

The RFC states that its contents amount to a transposition of ETSI TS 101 733 V.1.7.4 and are maintained by ETSI.
sections.eli5: Imagine signing a contract and wanting it to still be believable twenty years from now. This document explains how to sign so the proof does not spoil.

sections.title: Parties, Policies and Validation
sections.content:
Four kinds of party appear: the signer, the verifier, Trusted Service Providers (TSPs) and an arbitrator who settles disputes. TSPs include certification authorities, registration authorities, CRL issuers, OCSP responders, repository authorities, time-stamping and time-marking authorities, and signature policy issuers.

A signature policy sets technical rules for validating a signature. If the verifier's policy is indicated by the signer or implied by the data, results are consistent. If it is missing or incomplete, different verifiers, including arbitrators, may get different results, so comprehensive policies are recommended. The RFC does not mandate their use.

Validation ends in one of three states: invalid (bad format, failed digital signature check, or a certificate known to be invalid or revoked), incomplete validation (status currently unknown, for example because certificates are missing or a grace period has not ended) or valid. An incomplete signature can be checked again later.
sections.eli5: There is the person who signs, the person who checks, helpers who vouch for people and clocks, and a judge if they disagree. Rules written down in advance make everyone reach the same answer.

sections.title: Basic Signatures and Their Attributes
sections.content:
Conformance requires the signer to create one of two basic forms. A CAdES-BES holds the signed data, mandatory signed attributes, the signature value and optional extras. A CAdES-EPES is a BES that also carries a signed signature-policy-identifier, naming the policy that must be used to validate it. The BES satisfies the legal requirements for electronic signatures under the European Directive, giving basic authentication and integrity, but on its own it lacks the information for longer-term verification.

Three signed attributes are mandatory: content-type, message-digest and one of signing-certificate (SHA-1 only) or signing-certificate-v2 (any digest algorithm, from RFC 5035). Exactly one signing-certificate attribute must be present. It identifies the signer's certificate by a compact hash, which guards against substitution and reissue attacks, and if the hash does not match the certificate used the signature is invalid. The older other-signing-certificate attribute from RFC 3126 is deprecated.

Optional signed attributes include signing-time (the time claimed by the signer), commitment-type-indication, signer-location, signer-attributes (a claimed or certified role) and content-time-stamp, a token proving the data existed before signing. The generic commitment types defined include proof of origin, receipt, delivery, sender, approval and creation. Several signatures can be independent or embedded, and a countersignature is a signature over another signature.
sections.eli5: The simplest signature is your name plus a note about which exact ID card you used. You may also write why you signed, such as approving or receiving something.

sections.title: Adding Validation Data for the Long Term
sections.content:
Validation data means the certificates, revocation status (CRLs or OCSP) and trusted time evidence needed to check a signature later. Each longer-lived form adds unsigned attributes to the one below.

  • CAdES-T adds trusted time: a signature-time-stamp over the signature value, or a time-mark kept by a trusted provider.
  • CAdES-C adds complete-certificate-references and complete-revocation-references, which point to the certification path and the CRLs or OCSP responses used. Storing references lets the values live elsewhere.
  • CAdES-X variants add copies of the values (certificate-values, revocation-values) and time-stamps over the CAdES-C data. Types 1 and 2 counter the same threats, such as later compromise of a CA, CRL or OCSP key.
  • CAdES-A adds one or more archive-time-stamp attributes over the signed data, certificates, revocation data and all signer attributes. Successive stamps protect against weak hashing or broken cryptography, and the RFC says they should use stronger algorithms or longer keys than the originals.

A grace period lets revocation information propagate before a verifier builds CAdES-C, so it can be sure a certificate was not revoked at the time of the time-stamp. Trusted time should be as close as possible to signing, and must be created before the certificate is revoked or expires.

For arbitration, a CAdES-C is usable if conditions hold: the referenced data can be found, the time-stamping certificate is valid and unrevoked, no relevant private key was ever compromised, and the cryptography has not been broken.
sections.eli5: It is like sealing a letter in an envelope, then putting the envelope in a bigger sealed envelope with a dated postmark each time. Every layer proves the layer before it was fine.

sections.title: Conformance Requirements
sections.content:
Signers must implement at least one of CAdES-BES or CAdES-EPES. For a BES, the minimum is CMS SignedData with version 3 and at least one SignerInfo, the content-type and message-digest attributes, and one of the two signing-certificate attributes. An EPES adds signature-policy-identifier. Having no signers is not valid.

Verifiers must support one of two routes, both only up to CAdES-C. With time-stamping, they support the signature-time-stamp and the certificate and revocation reference attributes plus X.509 certificates and either CRLs or OCSP. With secure records, they instead keep a tamper-evident record of when the signature was first validated. The extended (CAdES-X) and archive (CAdES-A) forms are not needed to conform.
sections.eli5: To follow the rules you only need to make or check the basic stamped version. The extra long-life layers are optional extras.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Annex E gives two points. The security of the mechanism depends on the privacy of the signer's private key, so implementations should take steps to ensure private keys cannot be compromised. Cryptographic algorithms also become weaker with time, so implementations should be modular and ready for the set of mandatory-to-implement algorithms to change.

The long-term formats themselves exist to address these risks: time-stamps fix when a signature existed, and archive time-stamps renew protection as algorithms and keys age.
sections.eli5: Keep your pen safe, because anyone with it can sign as you. Also remember that locks get easier to pick over time, so be ready to swap in a better one.
